Myths & Facts

Correcting information. Reducing distance.

HIV myths are not harmless mistakes. They can fuel fear, social distance, discrimination, avoidance of testing or care, and treatment that undermines dignity.

Myth

HIV is transmitted through hugging or shaking hands.

Fact

HIV is not transmitted through everyday social contact.

Hugging, shaking hands, touching or being in the same room does not transmit HIV.

Why is this myth harmful?

It can cause people living with HIV to be excluded at home, school, work or in public places for no medical reason.

Myth

Sharing food, cutlery or a toilet can transmit HIV.

Fact

HIV is not transmitted through food, water, plates, glasses, cutlery or shared toilets.

Why does this matter?

Refusing to share meals or facilities can become exclusion in everyday life.

Myth

Mosquito bites can transmit HIV.

Fact

HIV is not transmitted by mosquitoes, ticks or other insects.

HIV requires particular body fluids and routes for transmission; insects are not a route of HIV transmission.

The effect of misinformation

This myth draws attention away from how HIV is actually transmitted and from prevention choices that work.

Myth

You can tell someone’s HIV status by looking at them.

Fact

Appearance cannot show HIV status. Only an HIV test can determine it.

Why are assumptions harmful?

Judging by someone’s face, body, identity, occupation or relationships creates prejudice and false reassurance.

Myth

HIV and AIDS are the same thing.

Fact

HIV is a virus. AIDS is the most advanced stage of HIV infection.

With effective ART, HIV can be managed as a chronic condition and does not have to progress to AIDS.

Why does the distinction matter?

Equating HIV with AIDS can make a diagnosis sound like a conclusion about the future, even though effective treatment has changed the course of HIV.

Myth

ART cures HIV, so treatment can stop once someone feels well.

Fact

ART suppresses HIV but does not cure HIV infection.

Decisions about a regimen or stopping medicine should be discussed with a qualified health professional. Do not change treatment based only on general website information.

Why is this myth harmful?

Treating ART as a short, one-time cure can disrupt treatment engagement and viral-load monitoring.

U=U

Myth

“A person living with HIV always transmits HIV to sexual partners.”

Fact: A person taking ART who maintains an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV through sex.

U=U concerns sexual transmission. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, shared injecting equipment and treatment interruption require separate clinical guidance.

Myth

People living with HIV cannot plan a pregnancy.

Fact

Treatment and clinical care can greatly reduce the risk of HIV transmission during pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding.

Reproductive decisions, treatment choices, delivery and infant feeding should be discussed with a care team familiar with Indonesian guidance and the individual situation.

Why does this need care?

The myth can remove hope and autonomy. At the same time, clinical answers should not be reduced to a slogan or treated as identical to U=U’s evidence for sexual transmission.
